architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added an optional `experimental_encoder` configuration to WebSocket client and server adapters, maintaining JSON as the default for backward compatibility
architecture_decisions.rationale: The feature needed to be opt-in and non-breaking for existing users. By making it experimental and optional, we can gather feedback before stabilizing the API. The encoder interface is minimal (encode/decode methods) to support various binary formats while keeping the API surface small.
alternatives_considered: Separate WebSocket link for binary formats

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Created a shared Encoder interface that can handle both text (JSON) and binary (MessagePack, CBOR) formats, with proper type safety
architecture_decisions.rationale: The encoder needs to work across client and server boundaries with consistent behavior. The interface accepts string | Uint8Array for encode and string | ArrayBuffer | Uint8Array for decode, covering all WebSocket message types. This ensures compatibility with both text and binary WebSocket frames.
alternatives_considered: Separate interfaces for text vs binary encoders
Using MIME types for content negotiation
Relying solely on WebSocket's binaryType property

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added validation to ensure encoder compatibility between client and server, with clear error messages for mismatched configurations
architecture_decisions.rationale: When a binary encoder is used on one side but not the other, or when JSON encoder receives binary data, users need clear error messages. The implementation includes runtime checks in both jsonEncoder and custom encoders to detect format mismatches early.

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Maintained PING/PONG handling as text frames regardless of encoder configuration to preserve WebSocket keep-alive functionality
architecture_decisions.rationale: PING/PONG frames are part of the WebSocket protocol and must remain as text frames for compatibility with existing infrastructure and WebSocket libraries. The implementation checks for these control messages before passing data to the encoder.
alternatives_considered: Encoding PING/PONG with the custom encoder
Removing PING/PONG entirely for binary encoders

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Created a comprehensive example demonstrating MessagePack encoder usage with proper handling of undefined values and binary data
architecture_decisions.rationale: Developers need a working reference implementation to understand how to implement custom encoders. The example shows practical concerns like handling undefined values (which MessagePack converts to null) and configuring both client and server with the same encoder.
alternatives_considered: Simple code snippets without full context

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added comprehensive test suite covering encoder compatibility, binary encoding, and edge cases
architecture_decisions.rationale: Custom encoders introduce new failure modes that need to be tested. The test suite verifies that JSON encoder rejects binary data, binary encoders work correctly, and mismatched configurations produce appropriate errors.

implementation_summary:
The implementation adds experimental support for custom WebSocket encoders to tRPC, allowing developers to use binary formats like MessagePack, CBOR, or protobufs instead of JSON for WebSocket communications. The core design centers around a minimal Encoder interface with encode/decode methods that sits between the transformer and WebSocket transport layer.

Key architectural decisions include: 1) Making the feature opt-in via an experimental_encoder option to maintain backward compatibility, 2) Keeping PING/PONG control messages as text frames regardless of encoder choice to preserve WebSocket protocol compatibility, 3) Providing clear error messages when encoder configurations mismatch between client and server, and 4) Including a comprehensive example with MessagePack that demonstrates practical concerns like handling undefined values (which MessagePack converts to null but tRPC expects as undefined).

The implementation follows tRPC's existing patterns by adding the encoder configuration to both client WebSocket options and server WebSocket adapter options. The encoder processes data after transformer serialization on the client and before transformer deserialization on the server, maintaining the existing transformer abstraction for data shaping while allowing different wire formats. The example application shows a complete Next.js setup with WebSocket subscriptions using MessagePack, providing developers with a reference implementation that includes proper error handling and configuration.
